slides.text: Patient 09 came to my sleep clinic complaining of waking up every morning with bruised knuckles and soil under his fingernails. I wired twenty-four electrodes to his scalp, locked him inside Observation Suite B—four floors underground with no cellular signal—and watched the polysomnograph monitors from behind the one-way glass.

At 3:14 AM, his brainwaves dropped into deep delta sleep. Yet on the infrared camera, Patient 09 sat bolt upright in bed, eyes shut, and picked up the unplugged plastic courtesy phone on the nightstand. In a voice two octaves lower than his own, he began reciting a string of latitude and longitude coordinates, pausing every ten seconds as if listening to a reply.

I leaned toward the intercom microphone to wake him, but before my finger touched the switch, Patient 09 slowly turned his head toward the one-way mirror, smiled with his eyes still sealed shut, and spoke in my late father’s exact cadence: 'Don't press the button, Claire. We just finished digging the hole at those coordinates—and your car is still in the parking garage.'
